title: Don't crowd them
hookLine: don't cramp people's homes or weary their lives (Tao Te Ching 72)

cards: A teenager's bedroom door, closed. On the other side, a parent with a question, a reminder and a worry, all lined up. Knock now, and the door may stay closed for a week.
Wait an hour, and it might open on its own. Either side of that door is a hard place to stand. Chapter seventy-two of the Tao Te Ching is written to rulers, but it's about that hallway.

teach.b: First, the warning. When people no longer fear what's fearsome, the chapter opens, something far more fearsome arrives. Pile on enough pressure and the pressure stops working, and what comes next is worse.
Don't cramp the places where people live; don't weary the lives they lead. The old words are physical: don't press in on their dwellings, don't make them sick of living.

Then a neat loop: only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you. Third, the sage's own room. The sage knows himself but doesn't put himself on show, and cares for himself but doesn't set himself up high.
Someone who doesn't need to be seen, or to be above, has less reason to crowd anyone else. Fourth, the week, which ends here. Rivers and seas lead because they lie lower.
Three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward.
Coarse cloth with jade inside. Knowing you don't know.

teach.h: A WEEK OF TAKING LESS SPACE.
teach.b: Today fits the run: they're all ways of taking up less space so others have more.
Room looks like a question asked once instead of three times, a plan left open for someone else to fill, not reading over a shoulder.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-two as advice on governing and on any kind of authority: don't press in on people's homes or lives, and they won't turn against you.

o: a rule against large crowds gathering in public
leaving people room instead of pressing in on them
keeping strangers out so a city stays uncrowded

games.q: this week in the Tao Te Ching: tap the pairs.

s: chapter seventy-two says more pressure keeps people in line
it warns that when people stop fearing what's fearsome, something worse arrives.
the chapter says if you don't weary people, they won't weary of you
it's a loop: give room, and you're given room back.
the sage in chapter seventy-two puts himself on show
the sage knows himself but doesn't display himself, and cares for himself without setting himself high.

games.q: you have authority over others and they've grown tired of you. what does chapter seventy-two advise?
o: press harder so they fear you again.
stop cramping their homes and wearying their lives.
games.why: the chapter says don't cramp where they live or weary their lives. only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you.

practice: Let your breath find its own pace, giving it room too, and bring to mind one person you've been pressing on, even gently: a child, a partner, a coworker, a friend who owes you a reply.
Picture the space around them, and ask what you could stop asking, checking or reminding, just for today. Rest with the space that leaves.

wordCard.voice: Don't crowd them. Chapter seventy-two: don't cramp where people live or weary the lives they lead; if you don't weary them, they won't weary of you. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: don't press in on where they live, from chapter seventy-two.

carryVoice: Your line: give room. Less pressure leaves more space for them to come to you. Until next time.
